topic: Parler des Gens que l'on Admire Beaucoup (Talking About People We Greatly Admire)

subUnits.title: 6.1 Vocabulaire et les Verbes Aimer et Admirer
notes: Vocabulaire et les Verbes Aimer et Admirer
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: describe qualities admired in others, and use the verb admirer alongside aimer.
Key Concepts:
1. Admired Qualities (reviewed and new):
- REVIEWED: bon(ne) (good), gentil(le) (kind), honnête (honest — unchanging), intelligent(e) (intelligent)
- NEW: prudent(e) (careful/prudent)
2. New Verb — Admirer (to admire):
- ADMIRER follows the regular '-ER' pattern: j'admire, tu admires, il/elle admire, nous admirons, vous admirez, ils/elles admirent
- Combined with AIMER: J'aime bien mon professeur (I like my teacher — general) vs. J'admire son intelligence (I admire his/her intelligence — specific quality)
- J'admire + [NOUN form of quality]: j'admire son honnêteté, j'admire sa gentillesse
3. Aimer vs. Admirer:
- AIMER: general warm liking for a PERSON as a whole
- ADMIRER: focused praise of a SPECIFIC quality in that person
Formula Box:
admirer: j'admire | tu admires | il/elle admire | nous admirons | vous admirez | ils/elles admirent
j'admire + [noun quality]: j'admire son honnêteté (I admire his/her honesty)
j'admire la [quality] de [person]: j'admire la gentillesse de ma mère
Analogy:

Admirer is a more SPECIFIC, focused cousin of aimer: while 'aimer' expresses general warm liking for a PERSON, 'admirer' zooms in like a CAMERA LENS on one PARTICULAR quality you find genuinely impressive.
Common Mistakes to Avoid:
- Confusing 'aimer' (general liking of a person) with 'admirer' (focused praise of a specific quality).
- Treating 'admirer' as an irregular verb requiring separate memorisation — it is a regular -ER verb.

quiz.explanation: 'Prudent(e)' means careful or prudent — feminine adds -e: prudente.
'Admirer' means 'to admire' — it focuses on a specific quality, unlike the more general 'aimer.'

quiz.q: What is the correct conjugation of 'admirer' for 'je' (I)?
quiz.explanation: 'J'admire' — regular -ER pattern (note j' before vowel). Not 'je admire.'

quiz.q: What is the correct conjugation of 'admirer' for 'ils/elles'?
quiz.explanation: 'Ils/elles admirent' — regular -ER pattern, -ent ending for ils/elles.

quiz.q: What is the general difference between 'aimer' and 'admirer'?
opts: Admirer is used only for objects, never people
Aimer expresses general liking of a person; admirer focuses on a specific admired quality
They mean exactly the same, with no difference
Aimer is a stronger feeling than admirer
quiz.explanation: 'Aimer' is for general liking of a whole person; 'admirer' zooms in on a particular quality you find impressive.

quiz.q: How would you say 'I admire my mother's kindness'?
opts: J'aime la gentillesse de ma mère seulement
J'admire de la gentillesse ma mère
J'admire la gentillesse de ma mère
quiz.explanation: Use 'j'admire' + 'la [quality]' + 'de [person]': 'j'admire la gentillesse de ma mère.'

quiz.q: Admirer is compared to ___ in this week's analogy.
opts: a camera lens zooming in on one particular quality
a camera with no focus capability at all
a lens that only ever sees the whole picture, never a detail
quiz.explanation: Just as a camera lens can zoom in on one specific detail, 'admirer' focuses on one particular quality rather than the whole person.

opts: A verb with no fixed pattern
quiz.explanation: 'Admirer' is a regular -ER verb — conjugate it exactly as you would 'aimer' or 'adorer.'

quiz.q: How would you say 'he is a careful driver'?
quiz.explanation: 'Il est un chauffeur prudent' — note: when an adjective follows the noun, the article (un) IS used. The no-article rule applies only to être + profession alone.

quiz.q: This week's vocabulary once again draws heavily on ___.
opts: entirely new, unrelated words with no connection to prior learning
words met in earlier terms, reinforcing them cumulatively
quiz.explanation: Most of this week's quality vocabulary (bon, gentil, honnête, intelligent) comes from earlier terms — genuine fluency is built through cumulative reinforcement.
